p.src: Now it is told that at the king’s morning court, all the civil and military officials presented memorials and petitioned, “My lord, we beg you to pardon our breach of decorum.” The king said, “Your manners are as proper as ever. How have you breached decorum?” The officials said, “My lord, we know not why, but in a single night every hair on our heads has vanished.” Taking up this memorial concerning their hairless heads, the king descended from the dragon throne and told his ministers, “Indeed, no one knows why. Everyone in my palace, high and low, also lost all their hair overnight.” Sovereign and ministers alike shed streams of tears, saying, “From this day forth, we shall never again dare slaughter monks.” The king returned to the dragon throne, and the officials resumed their appointed ranks. The king then said, “Those with business, step forward and report; if there is none, roll up the blinds and dismiss the court.” At once the commander charged with patrolling the city stepped from the military ranks, while the commissioner of the Eastern Ward emerged from the civil ranks. They kowtowed before the steps and said, “By imperial command we patrolled the city, and last night we recovered a chest of stolen goods and one white horse. We dare not decide the matter on our own and beg Your Majesty to determine its disposal.” The king was delighted and said, “Bring the chest here with everything in it.”

At once the commander charged with patrolling the city stepped from the military ranks, while the commissioner of the Eastern Ward emerged from the civil ranks. They kowtowed before the steps and said, “By imperial command we patrolled the city, and last night we recovered a chest of stolen goods and one white horse.
We dare not decide the matter on our own and beg Your Majesty to determine its disposal.”
The king was delighted and said, “Bring the chest here with everything in it.”

p.src: The two officials immediately withdrew to their offices, mustered a well-ordered troop of soldiers, and had the chest carried out. Inside, Tripitaka was frightened out of his wits and said, “Disciples, when we are brought before the king, how shall we explain ourselves?” Pilgrim laughed. “Do not make a fuss. I have arranged everything. When they open the chest, he will acknowledge us as his masters. Only tell Bajie not to contend over who is senior or junior.” Bajie said, “So long as I escape execution, that alone is immeasurable good fortune. How would I dare contend over anything?” Before they had finished speaking, the chest was carried outside the court, through the Five Phoenix Tower, and set below the vermilion steps.

p.src: The two officials asked the king to inspect it, and he at once ordered it opened. The lid had scarcely been lifted when Zhu Bajie could restrain himself no longer and leaped out, terrifying the assembled officials so badly that their hearts quaked and they could not speak. Then they saw Sun Wukong help the Tang monk out, while Friar Sand brought out the luggage. Seeing the commander holding the horse, Bajie strode forward and barked, “That horse is mine. Hand it over!” The officer was so frightened that he tumbled head over heels and fell to the ground. All four pilgrims stood before the steps. When the king saw that they were four monks, he hastily descended from the dragon throne, summoned the consorts and queens of his three palaces, and left the Golden Throne Hall with them. Together with all his ministers he bowed and asked, “From whence have you come, venerable elders?” Tripitaka replied, “We were sent by the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Living Buddha at the Great Thunderclap Monastery in India in the West and obtain the true scriptures.” The king said, “Masters, having come from so far away, why were you resting inside this chest?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk knew that Your Majesty had vowed to kill monks. Not daring to enter your noble realm openly, we disguised ourselves as laymen and sought lodging last night at an inn in this blessed place. For fear that our true identities might be discovered, we therefore slept inside the chest. Unfortunately, thieves stole it away, only to be caught by the commander, who had us carried here. Now that we behold Your Majesty’s august countenance, it is truly as though the clouds have parted and revealed the sun. We pray that Your Majesty will pardon and release us; your grace would be as deep as the sea.” The king said, “Master, you are an eminent monk from the celestial empire, and I have failed to welcome you properly. It is true that for years I have vowed to kill monks. Once, a monk slandered me, so I made a vow to Heaven that I would kill ten thousand monks to fulfill it. Unexpectedly, tonight we were converted and made monks ourselves. Now the hair of sovereign, ministers, queens, and consorts has all been shaved away. We beg you, masters, not to withhold your lofty wisdom, but accept us among your disciples.” Hearing this, Bajie laughed aloud. “If you wish to become our disciples, what initiation gift will you offer?” The king said, “If the masters consent, I shall present you with all the treasures in the kingdom.” Pilgrim said, “Say no more of treasure. We monks are men who possess the Way. Simply exchange our travel rescript and escort us out of the city. Then may your imperial realm remain forever secure, and blessings and longevity ever increase.” On hearing this, the king immediately ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainments to prepare a magnificent banquet. Sovereign and ministers were united in heart and together embraced the one true faith. They exchanged the travel rescript at once and asked the master to give the kingdom a new name. Pilgrim said, “The name ‘Dharma Kingdom’ is excellent, Your Majesty, but the word ‘Destroyer’ is quite unsuitable. Since I have passed through your land, change its name to the ‘Kingdom That Reveres the Dharma.’ I guarantee that for a thousand generations your seas will be calm, your rivers clear, and throughout the realm the winds and rains will come in their proper seasons.” The king thanked him for this favor. He arrayed the full imperial escort and accompanied the Tang monk and his three disciples out of the city on their westward way. Of how sovereign and ministers followed goodness and returned to the truth, we shall say no more.

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Disciple, how could I not understand? According to those four lines, the thousands of sutras and myriad scriptures all amount to nothing more than cultivating the mind.” Pilgrim said, “No more need be said. When the mind is pure, its solitary radiance shines alone; when the mind is steadfast, all realms are clear. But stray the least bit into sloth and negligence, and success will not be attained in a thousand years or ten thousand ages. You need only be wholly sincere in your resolve, and Thunderclap will be right before your eyes. If you remain fearful and alarmed like this, with your mind unsettled, the Great Way is far away, and Thunderclap is far away as well. So harbor no foolish doubts, but follow me.” On hearing these words, the elder’s mind at once grew clear and refreshed, and all his anxieties ceased.

p.src: Master and disciples proceeded timidly and fearfully when suddenly they heard a roaring gust of wind arise. Tripitaka said fearfully, “The wind has risen.” Pilgrim said, “Spring has its gentle wind, summer its fragrant wind, autumn its golden wind, and winter its northern wind. There is wind in every season. What is there to fear when it rises?” Tripitaka said, “This wind has come with great violence. It certainly is not a natural wind.” Pilgrim said, “Since ancient times, wind has risen from the earth and clouds have issued from the mountains. How could there be any wind from heaven?”

p.src: He also saw thirty or forty lesser demons arrayed on either side beneath him, while the monster stood there working his magic, blowing out wind and belching forth mist. Wukong laughed to himself. “My master did have some foreknowledge. He said it was no natural wind, and sure enough, it is a fiend making all this commotion here. If old Sun brought his iron staff straight down upon him, it would be nothing but pounding garlic: I would certainly kill him, but only at the cost of old Sun’s good name.” All his life Wukong had been a hero and had never understood how to attack another by stealth. He thought, “I shall go back and give Zhu Bajie a little attention—have him come and fight this fiend first. If Bajie proves capable and strikes the fiend down, that will be his good fortune; if he lacks the skill and is captured, I shall go and rescue him afterward, and thus win myself a fine reputation. Besides, he is always putting on airs and shirking his work, never willing to step forward; only his appetite is keen, and he loves to eat. Let me trick him a little and see what he says.”

p.src: He immediately descended from the clouds and came before Tripitaka. Tripitaka asked, “Wukong, what fortune or peril lies within that wind and mist?” Wukong replied, “It is clear now. There is no wind or mist to speak of.” “Indeed,” said Tripitaka. “I can feel that it has subsided somewhat.” Wukong laughed. “Master, ordinarily my eyes serve me well, but this time I was mistaken. I thought there might be a monster in the wind and mist, but it turns out there is not.” “Then what is it?” asked Tripitaka. Wukong replied, “Not far ahead lies a village. Its people delight in doing good, and they are steaming white rice and wheaten buns as alms for passing monks. I expect this mist is the steam from their cooking pots, and also a sign of the merit they have amassed.” Hearing this, Bajie believed every word. He pulled Wukong aside and whispered, “Brother, did you already eat some of their alms food?” Wukong replied, “Not very much. The vegetables were rather too salty, so I did not care to eat more.” “Pah!” said Bajie. “However salty it may be, I will eat until my belly is full. If it makes me terribly thirsty, I can come back and drink water.” Wukong asked, “Do you want to eat?” “I do,” said Bajie. “I am a little hungry. How would it be if I went ahead and ate something first?” “Brother, say no more,” replied Wukong. “The ancient books say, ‘While the father is present, the son may not act on his own authority.’ With Master here, who would dare go ahead of him?” Bajie laughed. “If you say nothing, I will simply go.” Wukong said, “I shall say nothing. Let me see how you manage to leave.” That fool was especially resourceful where food was concerned. He stepped forward, made a deep obeisance, and said, “Master, Elder Brother just said that a family in the village ahead is giving alms to monks. But look at this horse: if we impose upon that household for both fodder and grain, would that not be troublesome? Fortunately, the wind and mist have now cleared. Rest here a while, and let me find some tender grass and feed the horse first; afterward we can go to that household to beg our meal.” The Tang Monk was delighted. “Excellent! What has made you so diligent today? Go quickly and return quickly.”

p.src: The fool walked off, laughing secretly to himself. Wukong caught up with him and pulled him back. “Brother, they give alms only to handsome monks, not ugly ones.” Bajie said, “In that case, I shall have to transform again.” “Exactly,” said Wukong. “Transform yourself before you go.” The fine fool also possessed thirty-six transformations. Entering a hollow in the mountain, he formed the hand sign, recited a spell, shook himself once, and changed into a short, thin monk. He struck a wooden fish in his hand and hummed away, but since he knew no sutras, all he could drone was, “The great man above.”

p.src: Meanwhile, the monster gathered in the wind and mist, gave orders to his demon horde, and deployed them in a circular formation at the main road, there to await travelers. The luckless fool soon blundered right into their midst. The demons surrounded him: one seized his robe, another caught his silken sash, and all of them jostled and shoved as they laid hands on him together. “Do not pull me,” said Bajie. “Let me eat my way through your houses one by one.” The demons asked, “Monk, what do you mean to eat?” Bajie replied, “You provide alms for monks here, so I have come to eat an alms meal.” The demons said, “You imagine that monks are fed here, but you do not know that here we make a point of eating monks. We are all demon immortals who attained the Way in these mountains. We make a practice of carrying you monks home, steaming you in a steamer, and eating you cooked. And still you think you have come for an alms meal!” At these words Bajie grew frightened and began cursing Wukong in his heart. “That Protector of the Horses is truly a wretched scoundrel. He tricked me by saying the villagers here gave alms to monks, but where is there any village household in this place? Who here is providing any alms for monks? So it was these fiends all along!” When their tugging became too much, the fool instantly resumed his true form, drew the rake from his waist, and struck wildly until he drove the lesser demons back.

p.src: When the fiend heard this, he shouted, “So you are a disciple of the Tang Monk! I have long heard that the Tang Monk’s flesh is delicious, and I have been meaning to capture you. Now that you have blundered into my hands, do you think I will spare you? Do not flee! Take my cudgel!” Bajie said, “You vile beast! So you began your career as a master dyer.” The fiend asked, “How am I a master dyer?” Bajie replied, “If you were not a master dyer, how would you know how to wield a pounding club?” The monster would tolerate no more words and rushed forward, striking wildly. The two fought in the mountain hollow, and a splendid battle it was:

p.src: Meanwhile, behind the Tang Monk, Wukong suddenly let out a derisive laugh. Sha Monk asked, “Brother, why do you laugh so?” Wukong replied, “Zhu Bajie truly is a fool. The moment he heard that monks were being fed, he let me trick him into going. He has still not returned after all this time. If he beats back the fiends with a flurry of his rake, just watch him come back victorious, clamoring about his achievement; but if he cannot defeat them and is captured, that will be my misfortune—whether to my face or behind my back, who knows how many times he will have cursed that Protector of the Horses! Wujing, say nothing. Let me go and have a look.”

p.src: What a splendid Great Sage! Without letting the elder know, he quietly plucked a hair from the back of his head, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly changed into his own likeness and accompanied Sha Monk beside the elder. His true body sent forth its spirit and leapt into the air to observe. He saw the fool surrounded by monsters, swinging his rake wildly and gradually finding himself outmatched. Unable to bear it, the Pilgrim lowered his cloud and shouted sternly, “Do not panic, Bajie! Old Sun is here!” When the fool heard the Pilgrim’s voice, he took heart and grew fiercer than ever, laying about him with his rake and striking wildly ahead. The monster could not withstand him and said, “This monk was no match for us before. Why has he suddenly turned so fierce?” Bajie said, “You whelps, do not think you can bully me. One of my family has come!” He pressed forward all the harder, striking indiscriminately at heads and faces. The monster was utterly unable to parry him and led the lesser fiends away in defeat. Seeing the monsters retreat, the Pilgrim did not approach any closer. He wheeled his cloud around, returned directly to his original place, shook the hair, and took it back onto his body. The elder, with his mortal eyes and fleshly body, could never have recognized what had happened.

p.src: Before long, the fool returned victorious, so exhausted that sticky drool and mucus ran from him and white foam bubbled at his mouth. He came panting up and called, “Master!” Seeing him, the elder asked in surprise, “Bajie, you went to cut fodder for the horse. Why have you come back in such a sorry state? Could it be that someone from a household on the mountain was guarding it and would not let you cut the grass?” The fool put down his rake, beat his chest, stamped his feet, and said, “Master, do not ask. The mere telling of it would shame me to death.” The elder asked, “What is there to be ashamed of?” Bajie said, “Elder Brother played a trick on me. Earlier he said that the shapes in the wind and mist were not monsters and held no evil omen, but belonged to a charitable village household steaming white rice and white-flour buns as alms for monks. I believed him. Since I was hungry, I thought I would go ahead and beg for some, pretending that I was only there to cut grass. Who could have known that a whole host of monsters would surround me? I fought bitterly for all this time, and had Elder Brother’s mourning staff not come to my aid, I could never have escaped their snare and returned.” The Pilgrim laughed from beside him and said, “This fool is talking nonsense. When you turn thief, you implicate everyone in the same jail. I have been here watching over Master. When did I ever leave his side?” The elder said, “That is true. Wukong never left me.” The fool jumped up and cried, “Master, you do not understand—he has a substitute body!” The elder asked, “Wukong, are there truly monsters there?”

p.src: Unable to conceal it any longer, the Pilgrim bowed and said with a smile, “There are one or two minor fiends, but they dare not provoke us. Bajie, come here. I will look after you all the more. Since we are escorting Master across steep and perilous mountain roads, we must act like an army on the march.” Bajie asked, “And what does marching as an army mean?” The Pilgrim said, “You shall be the path-clearing general and open the road ahead. If the monster does not come, so much the better. If he does, fight him, and when you strike him down, the merit shall be yours.” Bajie reckoned that the monster’s abilities were about equal to his own and said, “Even if I die at his hands, so be it. Let me go first.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “This fool begins with words of ill omen. How can he ever make progress?” Bajie said, “Brother, you know the saying: when a young lord attends a banquet, if he is not drunk, he is at least full; when a brave man enters battle, if he does not die, he comes away wounded. Speak a mistaken word beforehand, and afterward you can display your might.” Delighted, the Pilgrim at once saddled the horse and invited Master to mount. Sha Monk shouldered the luggage, and together they followed Bajie into the mountains. Of their journey we shall say no more for now.

p.src: Now the monster, leading the few battered fiends who had survived the rout, went straight back to his cave. He sat high upon the rocky ledge, silent and brooding. Many lesser fiends had remained behind to guard the cave. They all came forward and asked, “Your Majesty usually returns cheerfully whenever you go out. Why are you troubled today?” The old monster said, “Little ones, whenever I used to leave the cave to patrol the mountain, no matter where I went, I would always seize a few men or beasts and bring them home to feed you. Today my luck was poor, and I encountered a formidable foe.” The lesser fiends asked, “What foe was that?” The old monster said, “A monk named Zhu Bajie, a disciple of the Tang Monk from the Eastern Land who is journeying to obtain the scriptures. He gave me such a thrashing with his nine-pronged rake that I was driven from the field in defeat. How infuriating! For some time I have often heard it said that the Tang Monk is an arhat cultivated through ten lifetimes, and that whoever eats a piece of his flesh can prolong his years and live forever. Unexpectedly, he has come to my mountain today. It would be the perfect chance to seize and steam him for food, but I never knew he had such a disciple under his command.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, a lesser fiend stepped out from among the ranks. Facing the old monster, he sobbed and wept three times, then chuckled and laughed three times. The old monster shouted, “Why are you both crying and laughing?” The lesser fiend knelt and said, “Your Majesty just spoke of eating the Tang Monk, but his flesh is not fit to be eaten.” The old monster said, “Everyone says that eating a piece of his flesh grants immortality and a lifespan equal to Heaven’s. Why do you say he is not fit to eat?” The lesser fiend said, “If he were fit to eat, he would never have reached this place; monsters elsewhere would already have eaten him. He has three disciples under his command.” The old monster asked, “Do you know those three?” The lesser fiend said, “His eldest disciple is Sun the Pilgrim, his third disciple is Sha Monk, and this one is his second disciple, Zhu Bajie.” The old monster asked, “How does Sha Monk compare with Zhu Bajie?” The lesser fiend replied, “There is not much difference between them.” “And how does Sun the Pilgrim compare with them?” The lesser fiend stuck out his tongue and said, “I dare not say. That Sun the Pilgrim possesses vast supernatural powers and countless transformations. Five hundred years ago he caused havoc in the Celestial Palace. The Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions above, the Nine Luminary Star Lords, the Twelve Zodiac Deities, the five ministers and four chancellors, the eastern and western constellations, the divine lords of north and south, the gods of the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers, and all the divine generals beneath Heaven could not prevail against him. How dare you think of eating the Tang Monk?” The old monster asked, “How do you know all this in such detail?” The lesser fiend said, “I once lived with the kings in the Lion-Camel Cave on Lion-Camel Ridge. Those kings, not knowing what was good for them, sought to eat the Tang Monk. Sun the Pilgrim stormed through the gate wielding his gold-hooped staff, and the poor creatures were beaten into the names of domino combinations—all ‘broken aces and severed sixes.’ Fortunately, I had enough sense to escape through the rear gate. I came here and was graciously taken in by Your Majesty. That is how I know what he can do.” On hearing this, the old monster turned pale with alarm. This was truly a case of “the great general fearing an ominous prophecy.” Having heard one of his own followers speak this way, how could he not be frightened?

p.src: While they were all trembling with fear, another little demon stepped forward and said, “Your Majesty, do not be angry or afraid. As the saying goes, ‘Things should be approached at leisure.’ If you wish to eat the Tang Monk, let me devise a plan to capture him.” The old demon asked, “What plan have you?” The little demon replied, “I have a plan called the Parted Plum Blossom.” The old demon asked, “What do you mean by the ‘Parted Plum Blossom Plan’?” The little demon said, “Now muster every demon in the cave, great and small; choose a hundred from a thousand, ten from a hundred, and only three from the ten. They must be capable fellows skilled in transformation. Let them all assume Your Majesty’s appearance, wear your helmet and armor, wield your cudgel, and lie in ambush at three places. First send one to fight Zhu Bajie, another to fight Sun the Novice, and the third to fight Sha the Monk. By sacrificing three little demons, we can lure all three disciples away. Then Your Majesty can reach down from midair with a cloud-seizing hand and snatch the Tang Monk. It will be as easy as taking something from your own pocket, or plucking a fly from a basin of water. What difficulty could there be?” The old demon was delighted to hear this and cried, “A marvelous plan! Marvelous indeed! If we fail to capture the Tang Monk on this expedition, so be it; but if we capture him, I shall reward you handsomely and appoint you vanguard of the front division.” The little demon kowtowed in gratitude and called for the demons to be mustered. All the spirits in the cave, great and small, were assembled, and sure enough three capable little demons were chosen. Each transformed into the old demon, took up an iron cudgel, and lay in ambush awaiting the Tang Monk. Of this we shall say no more for now.

p.src: Now the elder of the Tang, free from care and worry, followed Bajie onto the main road. After they had traveled for some time, there came a sudden crash beside the road, and a little demon leapt out and rushed forward to seize the elder. Sun the Novice shouted, “Bajie, a demon is here! Why don’t you strike?” The fool, unable to tell true from false, whipped out his rake, charged after it, and struck wildly. The demon raised its iron cudgel to parry him. As the two traded blows in fierce combat below the hillside, another crash came from the thicket. A second monster leapt out and rushed straight at the Tang Monk. The Novice said, “Master, this is bad! Bajie’s poor eyesight has let that demon through to seize you. Wait here while old Sun goes to fight it.” He hurriedly drew his staff, rushed forward, and shouted, “Where do you think you’re going? Take this!” The demon said not a word, but raised its cudgel to meet him. The two charged and clashed below the grassy slope and were locked in combat when a rush of wind sounded behind the mountain. Yet another demon leapt out and made straight for the Tang Monk. Sha the Monk saw it and exclaimed in alarm, “Master, both Elder Brother and Second Brother have been deceived! They have let the demon through to seize you. Stay seated on the horse while old Sha goes to capture it.” This monk too failed to distinguish friend from foe. He drew his staff at once and blocked the demon’s iron cudgel head-on. They grappled bitterly, shouting and bellowing as they fought in wild confusion, and gradually drew farther away. The old monster, watching from midair, saw the Tang Monk sitting alone upon his horse. He reached down with five claws like steel hooks and seized him in one grasp. The master fell from his horse, his feet slipping free of the stirrups, and the demon swept him away in a gust of wind. Alas, poor monk! It was truly as the saying goes:

p.src: The old demon descended on the wind and carried the Tang Monk into the cave, where he called, “Vanguard!” The little demon who had devised the plan came forward, knelt, and said, “I am unworthy, unworthy.” The old demon asked, “Why do you say that? Once a great general has given his word, it is as irreversible as dyeing white cloth black. I said then that if we failed to capture the Tang Monk, that would be the end of it, but if we captured him, I would appoint you vanguard of the front division. Today your ingenious plan has succeeded. How could I break faith with you? Bring the Tang Monk here, and have the underlings fetch water, scour the pot, carry in firewood, and light the fire so that we may steam him. You and I shall each eat a piece of his flesh and thereby gain long life and immortality.” The vanguard said, “Your Majesty, we must not eat him yet.” The old monster asked, “Now that we have captured him, why can we not eat him?” The vanguard replied, “It would be no great matter if Your Majesty ate him. Zhu Bajie can be dealt with, and Sha the Monk can be dealt with too. But I fear that vicious fellow Sun the Novice. If he learns that we ate his master, he will not even bother to fight us. He will simply thrust his golden-hooped staff into the mountainside, bore a hole through it, and overturn the whole mountain. Then we shall have no place left to shelter.” The old monster asked, “Vanguard, what wise counsel have you, then?” The vanguard replied, “If you follow my advice, send the Tang Monk to the rear garden, bind him to a tree, and give him no food for two or three days. First, that will cleanse his insides; second, we can wait and see whether his three disciples come searching at our gate. Once we learn that they have gone away, we can bring him out and enjoy him at our leisure. Would that not be best?” The old monster laughed. “Exactly, exactly! The vanguard speaks with reason.” At his command, the Tang Monk was taken into the rear garden and bound to a tree with a rope, while all the little demons went to the front to await orders.

p.src: Look at the elder, suffering under coils of rope, tightly and securely bound. Unable to stop the tears running down his cheeks, he cried, “My disciples, in what mountain are you capturing monsters, and along what road are you chasing demons? I have been captured by this vile fiend and suffer here. When shall we ever meet again? Oh, the agony!” As tears streamed from both his eyes, he suddenly heard someone call from a tree opposite, “Elder, have you been brought in here too?” The elder composed himself and asked, “Who are you?” The man replied, “I am a woodcutter from this mountain. The lord of the mountain captured me the day before yesterday and bound me here. It has now been three days, and I reckon he means to eat me.” The elder said through his tears, “Woodcutter, if you die, it concerns only yourself, and you have little to leave behind. But if I die, my death will not be free of guilt.” The woodcutter said, “Elder, you are a man who has left the world. You have neither parents above nor wife and children below. If you die, you die. What guilt could remain?” The elder replied, “I set out from the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. By imperial command of Emperor Taizong of the Tang, I was to pay homage to the living Buddha and obtain the true scriptures, so as to deliver the masterless, lonely souls of the netherworld. If I lose my life now, would I not leave the sovereign waiting in vain and betray all his ministers? Oh, the agony!”
As tears streamed from both his eyes, he suddenly heard someone call from a tree opposite, “Elder, have you been brought in here too?”
The elder composed himself and asked, “Who are you?”
The man replied, “I am a woodcutter from this mountain. The lord of the mountain captured me the day before yesterday and bound me here. It has now been three days, and I reckon he means to eat me.”
The elder said through his tears, “Woodcutter, if you die, it concerns only yourself, and you have little to leave behind. But if I die, my death will not be free of guilt.”
The woodcutter said, “Elder, you are a man who has left the world. You have neither parents above nor wife and children below. If you die, you die. What guilt could remain?”
